title: A second battery in California
hypothesis: The ERCOT battery's forecast and dispatch rules earn a diversifying return on CAISO too.
question: Does the same day-ahead price model, refitted on CAISO, earn enough on a 1 MW / 4 MWh battery to run as a second book, and does it move independently of ERCOT?
prior: CAISO prices follow solar output: cheap or negative around midday and high in the evening. That spread is large and regular, so a battery should earn steadily there, with different weather driving it than in Texas.
method: Same model code and settings as the ERCOT book, refitted walk-forward on CAISO (SP15 day-ahead price, t+24, four folds). The refit was first checked to reproduce the frozen ERCOT forecasts exactly.

Charge-aware dispatch for both grids: each day is planned hour by hour so the battery stays between empty and 4 MWh, with at most four charging and four discharging hours, 0.85 round trip, scored on settled prices. The earlier hour-ranking rule, which this plan replaced in the live book, is shown for reference.
Inclusion rule fixed in advance: net Sharpe above 2.0 after $5/MWh, net $/MW-yr above 0, charge inside 0 to 4 MWh every day, and daily P&L correlation with ERCOT below 0.5. Eight trials logged.
verdict_reason: CAISO cleared all four rules: net $19.6k/MW-yr, net Sharpe 23.2, and a daily P&L correlation of +0.08 with ERCOT. The two batteries together earn $45.3k a year net on 2 MW at a net Sharpe of 10.9, against 6.4 for ERCOT alone. CAISO's Sharpe is high because the solar spread repeats almost every day; perfect insight on the same grid scores 24.2, and December barely covers costs.
lessons: A regular spread gives a smooth return but a smaller one. CAISO earns less per MW than ERCOT and makes it up in steadiness.
A reproduction check before a new grid caught a wrong note about which model library made the frozen forecasts.
The charge-aware plan became the live ERCOT dispatch rule on 2026-10-16.
